claim: The study developed a new model of TDP43 proteinopathy using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons.
source: In this study, we describe the development of a new model of TDP43 proteinopathy using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and characterization of this model throughout.

claim: The model induces mislocalization of endogenous TDP43 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm without mutating the TDP43 gene or using chemical stressors.
source: Utilizing a genome engineering approach, we induced the mislocalization of endogenous TDP43 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm without mutating the TDP43 gene or using chemical stressors.
evidence: The manuscript describes the genome engineering approach and demonstrates TDP43 mislocalization without mutations or chemical stressors.

claim: The model successfully recapitulates key early and late pathological features of TDP43 proteinopathy, including neuronal loss, reduced neurite complexity, and cytoplasmic accumulation and aggregation of TDP43.
source: Our model successfully recapitulates key early and late pathological features of TDP43 proteinopathy, including neuronal loss, reduced neurite complexity, and cytoplasmic accumulation and aggregation of TDP43.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing these pathological features in the model.

claim: The loss of nuclear TDP43 leads to splicing defects.
source: Concurrently, the loss of nuclear TDP43 leads to splicing defects, while its cytoplasmic gain adversely affects microRNA expression.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data showing splicing defects upon TDP43 mislocalization.

claim: Cytoplasmic gain of TDP43 adversely affects microRNA expression.
source: Concurrently, the loss of nuclear TDP43 leads to splicing defects, while its cytoplasmic gain adversely affects microRNA expression.
evidence: The manuscript presents small RNA sequencing data showing altered microRNA expression.

claim: TDP43 is capable of sustaining its own mislocalization, thereby perpetuating and further aggravating the proteinopathy.
source: Strikingly, our observations suggest that TDP43 is capable of sustaining its own mislocalization, thereby perpetuating and further aggravating the proteinopathy.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing persistent TDP43 mislocalization after removal of the initial trigger (doxycycline withdrawal).

claim: ALS is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the relentless degeneration of motor neurons (MNs) in both the brain and spinal cord.
source: ALS is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the relentless degeneration of motor neurons (MNs) in both the brain and spinal cord (Brown and Al-Chalabi, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brown and Al-Chalabi, 2017.

claim: ALS degeneration precipitates a cascade of symptoms including muscle weakness, atrophy, and paralysis, eventually leading to respiratory failure and death, typically within three to five years after the onset of symptoms.
source: This degeneration precipitates a cascade of symptoms including muscle weakness, atrophy, and paralysis, eventually leading to respiratory failure and death, typically within three to five years after the onset of symptoms (Hardiman et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hardiman et al., 2017.

claim: In ALS patients, TDP43, which normally resides in the nucleus, becomes mislocalized, forming aggregates in the cytoplasm of neurons and glial cells.
source: In ALS patients, TDP43, which normally resides in the nucleus, becomes mislocalized, forming aggregates in the cytoplasm of neurons and glial cells (Neumann et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Neumann et al., 2006.

claim: TDP43 proteinopathy is implicated in the majority of ALS cases and is considered a central player in the disease's pathogenesis.
source: This phenomenon, termed TDP43 proteinopathy, is implicated in the majority of ALS cases and is considered a central player in the disease's pathogenesis (Ling et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ling et al., 2013.

claim: TDP43 proteinopathy is a common feature in multiple age-associated neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS, limbic-predominant age-related TDP43 encephalopathy (LATE), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: TDP43 proteinopathy is a common feature in multiple age-associated neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS, limbic-predominant age-related TDP43 encephalopathy (LATE), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) (de Boer et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to de Boer et al., 2020.

claim: TDP43 is an RNA-binding protein that plays a critical role in RNA metabolism, encompassing RNA splicing, stabilization, and transport.
source: TDP43 (encoded by TARDBP) is an RNA-binding protein that plays a critical role in RNA metabolism, encompassing RNA splicing (Donde et al., 2019; Polymenidou et al., 2011; Arnold, 2012; Ling et al., 2015), stabilization (Sidibé et al., 2021), and transport (Nagano et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2019), thus ensuring proper neuronal function (Gimenez et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recent studies have demonstrated cryptic exon (CE) inclusion triggered by loss of nuclear TDP43, especially in transcripts of important neuronal genes UNC13A and STMN2.
source: For example, recent studies have demonstrated cryptic exon (CE) inclusion triggered by loss of nuclear TDP43 (Ling et al., 2015), especially in transcripts of important neuronal genes UNC13A (Brown et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022) and STMN2 (Klim et al., 2019; Melamed et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TDP43 associates with the microRNA biogenesis machinery and affects microRNA expression.
source: Additionally, TDP43 associates with the microRNA biogenesis machinery and affects microRNA expression (Buratti et al., 2010; Kawahara and Mieda-Sato, 2012; Paez-Colasante et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Widespread dysregulation of microRNA levels has been reported in spinal tissue obtained post-mortem from sporadic ALS cases.
source: Accordingly, widespread dysregulation of microRNA levels has been reported in spinal tissue obtained post-mortem from sporadic ALS cases (Reichenstein et al., 2019; Emde et al., 2015; Figueroa-Romero et al., 2016; Gagliardi et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Current cellular models aimed at investigating TDP43 mislocalization involve mutating the TDP43 nuclear-localization signal, using mutant versions identified in familial ALS patients, or the use of pharmacological agents to induce stress.
source: Current cellular models aimed at investigating TDP43 mislocalization involve mutating the TDP43 nuclear-localization signal, using mutant versions identified in familial ALS patients, or the use of pharmacological agents to induce stress (Barmada et al., 2010; Zuo et al., 2021; Ziff et al., 2023; Walker et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TDP43 is found to be mutated in <0.5% of all ALS cases.
source: Overexpression may not represent physiological conditions, TDP43 is found to be mutated in <0.5% of all ALS cases, and pharmacological induction might induce events unrelated to the disease.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the prevalence of TDP43 mutations in ALS.

claim: CEs identified in ALS/FTD cases are poorly conserved beyond primates, making it challenging to investigate the contribution of splicing defects to ALS pathophysiology using animal models.
source: Furthermore, CEs identified in ALS/FTD cases are poorly conserved beyond primates, making it challenging to investigate the contribution of splicing defects to ALS pathophysiology using animal models (Baughn et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Baughn et al., 2023.

claim: Human induced pluripotent technology (iPSCs) offers a powerful platform that addresses some of these issues with animal models, enabling the development of human models of ALS in vitro.
source: Human induced pluripotent technology (iPSCs) offers a powerful platform that addresses some of these issues with animal models, enabling the development of human models of ALS in vitro (Giacomelli et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Giacomelli et al., 2022.

claim: A recent study employed sporadic ALS (spALS) spinal cord extracts to induce TDP43 proteinopathy in iPSC-derived MNs.
source: A recent study employed sporadic ALS (spALS) spinal cord extracts to induce TDP43 proteinopathy in iPSC-derived MNs (Smethurst et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Smethurst et al., 2020.

claim: The spALS spinal cord extract model's utility is limited by the small percentage of neurons showing TDP43 pathology and the difficulty in producing spALS spinal extracts consistently and in large quantities.
source: However, the model's utility is limited by the small percentage of neurons showing TDP43 pathology and the difficulty in producing spALS spinal extracts consistently and in large quantities.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the limitations of the spALS extract model.

claim: GFP was fused to the C-terminus of TARDBP in its endogenous locus in healthy control iPSCs using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing.
source: We fused green fluorescent protein (GFP) to the C-terminus of TARDBP in its endogenous locus in healthy control iPSCs using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing (Figure 1A) and selected iPSC clones with a homozygous knock-in (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genome editing procedure and references figures showing the results.

claim: The integration of GFP did not adversely impact the differentiation of iPSCs into motor neurons (MNs).
source: We initially ascertained that the integration of GFP did not adversely impact the differentiation of iPSCs into motor neurons (MNs).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing successful differentiation and normal marker expression.

claim: The edited iPSCs (with GFP integration) efficiently differentiated into MNs based on the expression of established MN markers - ISLET1 (ISL1) and neurofilament-M (NF-M).
source: Based on the expression of established MN markers - ISLET1 (ISL1) and neurofilament-M (NF-M) - we confirmed that the edited iPSCs (with GFP integration) efficiently differentiated into MNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunostaining data showing expression of MN markers.

claim: The TDP43-GFP knock-in MNs did not show significantly altered expression levels of TARDBP, UNC13A, and STMN2, nor did it cause any upregulation of cryptic transcripts in STMN2 or UNC13A.
source: Moreover, the TDP43-GFP knock-in MNs did not show significantly altered expression levels of TARDBP, UNC13A, and STMN2, nor did it cause any upregulation of cryptic transcripts in STMN2 or UNC13A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents RT-qPCR data showing no significant changes in gene expression or splicing.

claim: ~80% of the cells in TDP43-GFP MN culture immunostained positive for ISL1.
source: These engineered iPSCs, hereafter called TDP43-GFP iPSCs, were differentiated into MNs (called TDP43-GFP MNs) where ~80% of the cells in culture immunostained positive for ISL1.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantification of ISL1-positive cells.

claim: Expression of the control nanobody did not affect TDP43 localization from the nucleus.
source: Expression of the nanobody (deemed the control nanobody) did not affect TDP43 localization from the nucleus (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence images showing nuclear TDP43 with control nanobody.

claim: Expression of the NES-nanobody in the TDP43-GFP neurons caused relocation of the fusion protein to the cytoplasm with a concomitant loss in the nucleus.
source: Expression of the NES-nanobody in the TDP43-GFP neurons caused relocation of the fusion protein to the cytoplasm with a concomitant loss in the nucleus (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence images and quantification showing cytoplasmic TDP43 with NES nanobody.

claim: TDP43 mislocalization leads to reduced dendrite complexity and neuronal soma swelling.
source: We observed that TDP43 mislocalization leads to reduced dendrite complexity and neuronal soma swelling (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and an increase in cleaved caspase-3 activation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), which is an indicator of apoptosis.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantification of morphological features showing these defects.

claim: TDP43 mislocalization leads to an increase in cleaved caspase-3 activation, which is an indicator of apoptosis.
source: We observed that TDP43 mislocalization leads to reduced dendrite complexity and neuronal soma swelling (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and an increase in cleaved caspase-3 activation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), which is an indicator of apoptosis.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantification of cleaved caspase-3 levels.

claim: Expression of the nanobodies in unedited iPSCs did not lead to apoptosis activation or dendrite defects.
source: We confirmed that expression of the nanobodies in unedited iPSCs did not lead to apoptosis activation or dendrite defects, confirming that the observed phenotypes are due to TDP43 mislocalization (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents control data showing no effects in unedited cells.

claim: TDP43 puncta reminiscent of aggregates were observed in the cytoplasm of MNs displaying mislocalized TDP43 that varied in size and number across individual neurons.
source: Additionally, we observed TDP43 puncta reminiscent of aggregates in the cytoplasm of MNs displaying mislocalized TDP43 that varied in size and number across individual neurons (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript presents super-resolution microscopy images and quantification of TDP43 puncta.

claim: MNs expressing the NES nanobody exhibit characteristic splicing defects showing inclusion of cryptic exons in both UNC13A and STMN2 and a reduction in the abundance of canonical transcripts.
source: The results strikingly mirrored the commonly observed ALS profile, showing inclusion of cryptic exons in both UNC13A and STMN2 and a reduction in the abundance of canonical transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents RT-qPCR data showing these splicing changes.

claim: The primary axis of variance (90%) in transcriptomic analysis is related to the expression of the control and NES nanobody.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated that the primary axis of variance (90%) is related to the expression of the control and NES nanobody, while the much smaller second PC component is related to the two clones (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents PCA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis revealed differential expression of hundreds of genes with a fold change of ≥2 and false discovery rate (FDR)<0.01.
source: Our analysis revealed differential expression of hundreds of genes with a fold change of ≥2 and false discovery rate (FDR)<0.01, suggesting a profound impact of TDP43 dysfunction on the transcriptome of MNs (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript presents differential expression analysis results.

claim: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the differentially expressed genes highlighted a significant enrichment of pathways related to synaptic dysfunction and cytoskeletal defects in axons and dendrites amongst downregulated genes.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the differentially expressed genes highlighted a significant enrichment of pathways related to synaptic dysfunction and cytoskeletal defects in axons and dendrites amongst downregulated genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents GO enrichment analysis results.

claim: Upregulated genes were enriched for GO terms related to RNA processing, including the nonsense-mediated decay.
source: In contrast, upregulated genes were enriched for GO terms related to RNA processing, including the nonsense-mediated decay (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents GO enrichment analysis results.

claim: Leafcutter analysis identified alterations in the splicing of 175 genes, including UNC13A and STMN2 (ΔPSI >0.1, adjusted p-value <0.01).
source: Our analysis identified alterations in the splicing of 175 genes, including UNC13A and STMN2 (ΔPSI >0.1, adjusted p-value <0.01).
evidence: The manuscript presents alternative splicing analysis results.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis on genes with splicing defects identified a significant enrichment of terms related to synaptic development (FDR <0.01).
source: To gain functional insights into these splicing defects, we performed pathway enrichment analysis on affected genes, identifying a significant enrichment of terms related to synaptic development (FDR <0.01).
evidence: The manuscript presents pathway enrichment analysis results.

claim: Only 35% of the splicing changes were proximal to a TDP43 binding site.
source: Interestingly, only 35% of the splicing changes were proximal to a TDP43 binding site (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparison with TDP43 eCLIP data.

claim: The loss of TDP43 from the nucleus may be responsible for a subset of the observed splicing defects, but not all.
source: This suggests that the loss of TDP43 from the nucleus may be responsible for a subset of the observed splicing defects, but not all.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only 35% of splicing changes are near TDP43 binding sites.

claim: A total of 476 isoforms related to STMN2 were identified using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read sequencing.
source: Employing our FICLE pipeline (Leung et al., 2023), we identified a total of 476 isoforms related to STMN2.
evidence: The manuscript presents long-read sequencing analysis results.

claim: 40 STMN2 isoforms, accounting for 8.4% of the total, were characterized by a cryptic exon (CE) starting at chr8:80529057.
source: Notably, 40 isoforms, accounting for 8.4% of the total, were characterized by a cryptic exon (CE) starting at chr8:80529057 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents long-read sequencing analysis results.

claim: STMN2 isoforms with the CE were exclusively expressed in TDP43-GFP MNs that expressed the NES nanobody.
source: These isoforms with the CE were exclusively expressed in TDP43-GFP MNs that expressed the NES nanobody.
evidence: The manuscript presents long-read sequencing analysis results comparing control and NES conditions.

claim: Four CE-containing STMN2 isoforms manifested a novel exon, 114 bp in length, positioned upstream of the CE.
source: Surprisingly, four of these CE-containing isoforms manifested a novel exon, 114 bp in length, positioned upstream of the CE (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents long-read sequencing analysis results.

claim: At a stringent FDR threshold of 0.01 and ΔPSI >0.1, 90 genes were detected as alternatively spliced in cortical neuronal nuclei that showed a loss of TDP43 from ALS patient tissue post-mortem.
source: At a stringent FDR threshold of 0.01 and ΔPSI >0.1, we detected 90 genes as alternatively spliced in nuclei that showed a loss of TDP43 using Leafcutter.
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of publicly available patient data.

claim: Thirty-four out of 90 genes alternatively spliced in ALS patient nuclei were also detected in the iPSC model.
source: Thirty-four out of these 90 genes were also detected in our iPSC model (Figure 2D), indicating strong concordance between the iPSC model and patient data, despite the differences in sample origin and neuronal subtype.
evidence: The manuscript presents comparison between model and patient data.

claim: All 34 genes that overlapped between patient data and iPSC model displayed an identical splicing event.
source: Importantly, all 34 genes displayed an identical splicing event.
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from the comparison analysis.

claim: There is a significant overlap between splicing defects due to a global loss of TDP43 and the mislocalization model.
source: In accordance with the model that nuclear loss of TDP43 drives splicing changes, we observed a significant overlap between splicing defects due to a global loss of TDP43 and our mislocalization model (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparison with TDP43 knockdown data.

claim: A number of genes that displayed splicing changes due to TDP43 mislocalization were not affected by TDP43 KD (143 genes for the GSE121569 and 79 genes for the PRJEB42763 dataset).
source: However, a number of genes that displayed splicing changes due to TDP43 mislocalization were not affected by TDP43 KD in either dataset (143 genes for the GSE121569 and 79 genes for the PRJEB42763 dataset).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparison with TDP43 knockdown data.

claim: Nuclear loss of TDP43 alone cannot entirely explain the widespread defects in alternative splicing.
source: This indicates that nuclear loss of TDP43 alone cannot entirely explain the widespread defects in AS.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many splicing changes in the mislocalization model are not seen with TDP43 knockdown.

claim: 12 genes were identified that showed alternative splicing in both the iPSC model and ALS/FTD post-mortem tissue at stringent thresholds.
source: Our analysis identified 12 genes, including STMN2 and UNC13A, that we further investigated using RT-qPCR.
evidence: The manuscript describes the analysis criteria and validation approach.

claim: RT-qPCR confirmed alternative splicing events in all 12 genes identified, where 9/12 genes displayed a decrease in expression of their canonical transcript levels.
source: This confirmed AS events in all the genes identified, where 9/12 genes displayed a decrease in expression of their canonical transcript levels (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript presents RT-qPCR validation data.

claim: Doxycycline (1 µg/ml) triggered significant TDP43 mislocalization in the TDP43-GFP-NES MNs.
source: Dox (1 µg/ml) triggered significant TDP43 mislocalization in the TDP43-GFP-NES MNs, while the TDP43-GFP-CTRL MNs and the TDP43-GFP-NES MNs without Dox maintained nuclear TDP43 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing doxycycline-induced mislocalization.

claim: Cytoplasmic TDP43 puncta were observed in the NES line.
source: Furthermore, we observed cytoplasmic TDP43 puncta in the NES line (Figure 3C), and a significant increase in phosphorylated TDP43 without a change in the total TDP43 protein levels upon mislocalization (Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents microscopy images showing puncta.

claim: There was a significant increase in phosphorylated TDP43 without a change in the total TDP43 protein levels upon mislocalization.
source: Furthermore, we observed cytoplasmic TDP43 puncta in the NES line (Figure 3C), and a significant increase in phosphorylated TDP43 without a change in the total TDP43 protein levels upon mislocalization (Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents western blot data showing increased phosphorylated TDP43.

claim: TDP43 mislocalization alone did not induce significant levels of G3BP1+ stress granules (SG).
source: We noted that the TDP43 mislocalization alone did not induce significant levels of G3BP1+ stress granules (SG) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing lack of stress granules without sodium arsenite treatment.

claim: When treated with sodium arsenite, both control and NES MNs displayed cytoplasmic SG.
source: When treated with sodium arsenite, both control and NES MNs displayed cytoplasmic SG (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing stress granules with sodium arsenite treatment.

claim: In NES MNs treated with sodium arsenite, only a subset of cytoplasmic TDP43 puncta co-localized with G3BP1+ stress granules.
source: However, in NES MNs treated with SA, only a subset of cytoplasmic TDP43 puncta co-localized with G3BP1+ stress granules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing partial co-localization.

claim: TDP43 mislocalization was observed as early as 8 hr after Dox treatment.
source: Notably, we observed TDP43 mislocalization as early as 8 hr after Dox treatment (Figure 4A), which was accompanied by significant AS errors in all 12 genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents time-course immunofluorescence data.

claim: Significant alternative splicing errors in all 12 genes were observed at 8 hr after Dox treatment.
source: Notably, we observed TDP43 mislocalization as early as 8 hr after Dox treatment (Figure 4A), which was accompanied by significant AS errors in all 12 genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents time-course RT-qPCR data.

claim: Dysfunctional alternative splicing could be one of the incipient molecular events in ALS pathogenesis due to TDP43 mislocalization.
source: This suggests that dysfunctional AS could be one of the incipient molecular events in ALS pathogenesis due to TDP43 mislocalization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that splicing defects occur very early (8 hr) after TDP43 mislocalization.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of day 40 MNs uncovered splicing defects, including cryptic exon inclusions and isoform switching in 494 genes (adjusted p-value <0.01 and ΔPSI >0.1).
source: Transcriptomic analysis of day 40 MNs uncovered splicing defects, including cryptic exon inclusions and isoform switching in 494 genes (adjusted p-value <0.01 and ΔPSI >0.1), with significant enrichment in pathways related to synaptic function and the cytoskeleton (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq analysis results from the inducible model.

claim: Splicing defects in the inducible model showed significant enrichment in pathways related to synaptic function and the cytoskeleton.
source: Transcriptomic analysis of day 40 MNs uncovered splicing defects, including cryptic exon inclusions and isoform switching in 494 genes (adjusted p-value <0.01 and ΔPSI >0.1), with significant enrichment in pathways related to synaptic function and the cytoskeleton (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents pathway enrichment analysis results.

claim: Following Dox withdrawal, TDP43 localization was largely restored to the nucleus.
source: Following Dox withdrawal, TDP43 localization was largely restored to the nucleus. However, a subset of neurons retained cytoplasmic TDP43 even after 21 days (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data after doxycycline withdrawal.

claim: A subset of neurons retained cytoplasmic TDP43 even after 21 days following Dox withdrawal.
source: Following Dox withdrawal, TDP43 localization was largely restored to the nucleus. However, a subset of neurons retained cytoplasmic TDP43 even after 21 days (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data after doxycycline withdrawal.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy revealed persistent cytoplasmic TDP43 in some neurons despite near undetectable nanobody expression.
source: Super-resolution microscopy further revealed persistent cytoplasmic TDP43 in these neurons, despite near undetectable nanobody expression (Figure 5C), suggesting that in some cells, TDP43 mislocalization may become self-sustaining.
evidence: The manuscript presents super-resolution microscopy data showing persistent mislocalization without nanobody.

claim: In some cells, TDP43 mislocalization may become self-sustaining.
source: Super-resolution microscopy further revealed persistent cytoplasmic TDP43 in these neurons, despite near undetectable nanobody expression (Figure 5C), suggesting that in some cells, TDP43 mislocalization may become self-sustaining.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TDP43 remains mislocalized even after the nanobody is no longer detectable.

claim: Removal of the initial trigger may be insufficient to completely reverse TDP43 once it has been mislocalized.
source: Our data indicates that removal of the initial trigger may be insufficient to completely reverse TDP43 once it has been mislocalized.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some neurons retain cytoplasmic TDP43 after doxycycline withdrawal.

claim: Around 150 microRNAs were found to be significantly altered (FDR <0.01 and fold change ≥1.5) upon TDP43 mislocalization.
source: Around 150 microRNAs were found to be significantly altered (FDR <0.01 and fold change ≥1.5) upon TDP43 mislocalization.
evidence: The manuscript presents small RNA sequencing analysis results.

claim: The microRNAs miR-218 and miR-9 were downregulated in the model, which have previously been shown to be downregulated in ALS MNs.
source: Our data captured downregulation of the microRNAs miR-218, and miR-9, which have previously been shown to be downregulated in ALS MNs (Reichenstein et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript presents small RNA sequencing data and cites previous studies showing the same changes in ALS.

claim: Almost equal numbers of microRNAs were upregulated or downregulated upon TDP43 mislocalization.
source: Interestingly, these changes were not unidirectional; almost equal numbers of microRNAs were upregulated or downregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents small RNA sequencing analysis results.

claim: In the case of TDP43 knockdown, only one microRNA (miR-1249–3 p) exhibited a significant change (FDR <0.01 and a fold change of 1.5).
source: Specifically, in the case of TDP43 knockdown, only one microRNA (miR-1249–3 p) exhibited a significant change (FDR <0.01 and a fold change of 1.5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents small RNA sequencing analysis results from TDP43 knockdown experiments.

claim: There was a substantial overlap between microRNAs that were downregulated due to TDP43 mislocalization and those downregulated following TDP43 knockdown.
source: We observed a substantial overlap between microRNAs that were downregulated due to TDP43 mislocalization and those downregulated following TDP43 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene set enrichment analysis results.

claim: There was no significant overlap for microRNAs that were upregulated in both TDP43 mislocalization and knockdown scenarios.
source: However, we did not observe a significant overlap for microRNAs that were upregulated in both scenarios (Figure 3—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene set enrichment analysis results.

claim: Mislocalized TDP43 selectively affects the expression of a subset of microRNAs.
source: Our data suggest that mislocalized TDP43 selectively affects the expression of a subset of microRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of mislocalization versus knockdown on microRNA expression.

claim: The nuclear loss and cytoplasmic gain of TDP43 induce distinct molecular alterations within motor neurons that converge to hasten neuronal dysfunction and demise.
source: Additionally, these observations highlight the possibility that the nuclear loss and cytoplasmic gain of TDP43 induce distinct molecular alterations within motor neurons that converge to hasten neuronal dysfunction and demise.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mislocalization and knockdown have different effects on microRNA expression.

claim: Western blot analysis with the Cosmo Bio antibody clearly detected hyperphosphorylated TDP43 in whole-cell lysates.
source: To address this, we performed western blot analysis with the Cosmo Bio antibody, which clearly detected hyperphosphorylated TDP43 in whole-cell lysates (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The manuscript presents western blot data showing phosphorylated TDP43.

claim: TDP43 undergoes alternative splicing within exon 6 in response to induced hyperexcitability in iPSC-derived iNeurons, generating truncated proteins.
source: TDP43 undergoes alternative splicing within exon 6 in response to induced hyperexcitability in iPSC-derived iNeurons, generating truncated proteins. These isoforms are detected in lumbar motor neurons; however, their levels remained unchanged between ALS patients and healthy tissue (Weskamp et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weskamp et al., 2020.

claim: Western blot analysis, even 20 days after inducing TDP43 mislocalization, showed no truncated fragments.
source: However, western blot analysis, even 20 days after inducing TDP43 mislocalization, showed no truncated fragments.
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from western blot experiments.

claim: TDP43 mislocalization alone is insufficient to generate significant levels of truncated isoforms.
source: This suggests that TDP43 mislocalization alone is insufficient to generate significant levels of truncated isoforms.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that no truncated fragments were detected after mislocalization.

claim: The model paves the way for inquiries into the roles of non-neuronal cells, such as oligodendrocytes and astrocytes, which also exhibit TDP43 proteinopathy, in contributing to neuronal dysfunction in a cell non-autonomous manner.
source: Beyond neurons, our model paves the way for inquiries into the roles of non-neuronal cells, such as oligodendrocytes and astrocytes, which also exhibit TDP43 proteinopathy, in contributing to neuronal dysfunction in a cell non-autonomous manner (Barton et al., 2021; James et al., 2022; Smethurst et al., 2020; Licht-Murava et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and represents a potential application of the model.

claim: The model will enhance understanding of ALS and accelerate efforts into developing therapies against TDP43 proteinopathies.
source: We expect this model to not only enhance our understanding of ALS but also other TDP43 proteinopathies and accelerate efforts into developing therapies against these devastating neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the model.
